o: The miserable state of Jerusalem, the just consequences of its sins.
Jerusalem represented as a captive female, lamenting, and seeking the mercy of God.
bg: Called in the Hebrew canon 'Ekhah, meaning "How," being the formula for the commencement of a song of wailing. It is the first word of the book (see 2 Sam. 1:19-27).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The miserable state of Jerusalem, the just consequences of its sins (vv. 1–11); Jerusalem represented as a captive female, lamenting, and seeking the mercy of God (vv. 12–22). People named: Jacob. Places: Zion, Jerusalem, Judah.
ch.mh: The prophet sometimes speaks in his own person; at other times Jerusalem, as a distressed female, is the speaker, or some of the Jews.
q: Read verses 1–11 (The miserable state of Jerusalem, the just consequences of its sins). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 12–22 (Jerusalem represented as a captive female, lamenting, and seeking the mercy of God), what do you learn about suffering and endurance?
Verse 9 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Deuteronomy 32:29. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jacob’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of sin and repentance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Lamentations?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.a: Bring a present hardship to God and memorize the key verse as an anchor.

o: Lamentation for the misery of Jerusalem.
bg: Called in the Hebrew canon 'Ekhah, meaning "How," being the formula for the commencement of a song of wailing. It is the first word of the book (see 2 Sam. 1:19-27).
ch.s: This chapter covers: Lamentation for the misery of Jerusalem (vv. 1–22). People named: Jacob. Places: Zion, Jerusalem, Judah.
ch.mh: A sad representation is here made of the state of God's church, of Jacob and Israel; but the notice seems mostly to refer to the hand of the Lord in their calamities.
q: Read verses 1–22 (Lamentation for the misery of Jerusalem). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
Verse 19 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Psalms 62:8. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jacob’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of leadership and kingship in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Lamentations?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us fear God, and walk humbly before him, and take heed lest we fall.
ch.a: Let the seriousness of God's judgment move you to examine your ways and to pray for others.

o: The faithful lament their calamities, and hope in God's mercies.
bg: Called in the Hebrew canon 'Ekhah, meaning "How," being the formula for the commencement of a song of wailing. It is the first word of the book (see 2 Sam. 1:19-27).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The faithful lament their calamities, and hope in God's mercies (vv. 1–41).
ch.mh: The prophet relates the more gloomy and discouraging part of his experience, and how he found support and relief.
q: Read verses 1–41 (The faithful lament their calamities, and hope in God's mercies). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
Verse 25 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Micah 7:7–8. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of grace and mercy in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Lamentations?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We are apt, in times of calamity, to reflect on other people's ways, and blame them; but our duty is to search and try our own ways, that we may turn from evil to God.
ch.a: Encourage someone who is discouraged with a promise from this chapter.

o: The deplorable state of the nation is contrasted with its ancient prosperity.
bg: Called in the Hebrew canon 'Ekhah, meaning "How," being the formula for the commencement of a song of wailing. It is the first word of the book (see 2 Sam. 1:19-27).

Burning; the walled, a city in the vale of Siddim (Gen. 13:10; 14:1-16). The wickedness of its inhabitants brought down upon it fire from heaven, by which it was destroyed (18:16-33; 19:1-29; Deut. 23:17).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The deplorable state of the nation is contrasted with its ancient prosperity (vv. 1–22). People named: Uz. Places: Zion, Edom, Sodom, Jerusalem.
q: Read verses 1–22 (The deplorable state of the nation is contrasted with its ancient prosperity). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
Verse 20 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 2 Samuel 1:14. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Uz’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of judgment in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Lamentations?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Our anointed King alone is the life of our souls; we may safely live under his shadow, and rejoice in Him in the midst of our enemies, for He is the true God and eternal life.
ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.

o: The Jewish nation supplicating the Divine favour.
bg: Called in the Hebrew canon 'Ekhah, meaning "How," being the formula for the commencement of a song of wailing. It is the first word of the book (see 2 Sam. 1:19-27).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The Jewish nation supplicating the Divine favour (vv. 1–22). Places: Zion, Judah.
q: Read verses 1–22 (The Jewish nation supplicating the Divine favour). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
Verse 7 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Jeremiah 16:12. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Lamentations?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us watch against repinings and despondency; for we surely know, that it shall be well in the end with all that trust in, fear, love, and serve the Lord.
ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.
